To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
telephone buyers are the most loyal, frequent, and risk averse, whereas Internet third-party buyers are the least loyal, frequent, but most risk averse.

Internet-proprietary buyers are more similar to Internet-third party buyers than to telephone buyers in terms of their external search, number of considered alternatives, brand loyalty, frequency of purchase, and perceived risk of unavailability; however, telephone buyers are more similar than either Internet group in terms of Internet experience and usage, and they are also more likely to have used the Internet to search and book a trip.

telephone buyers employ less external search, consider fewer alternatives, are more loyal, are more frequent buyers and perceive less risk of unavailability, compared to Internet-proprietary buyers, who are in turn less loyal, more frequent buyers and more risk-averse compared to Internet-third party buyers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how consumers search for, evaluate, and select among consumer services.
the differences in consumer behavior across three purchase channels: Internet-proprietary, Internet-third party, and telephone.
how buyers use the various channels in making consumer services purchases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Internet-proprietary buyer is the most similar to the telephone buyer, whereas the Internet-third party buyer is the most dissimilar to the telephone buyer.
the Internet is not the panacea for all consumer services.
the three channels are different in terms of how consumers use them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Internet is not necessarily a panacea for all businesses, especially those that have a strong brand and a loyal customer base.
Internet-proprietary buyers fall in the middle of the other two channels in terms of all of the above factors.

Internet-third party sites are the most effective channel in terms of generating the greatest number of alternatives for buyers to consider, and the Internet-proprietary sites are most effective in terms of reducing risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the purchase channel influences the consumer services buyer’s behavior and that the channel is a significant factor in the consumer services buyer decision-making process.

the Internet-proprietary site buyers fall between the two extremes, which suggests that Internet-proprietary sites may have a difficult time differentiating from Internet-third party sites and from telephone.

consumers who buy through the Internet-proprietary channel have the same characteristics as those who buy through the telephone channel, while those who buy through Internet-third party channels are distinct.
